Northern District of Florida - 2026 filing fees, attorney fees, and real case data

Home » By District » Northern District of Florida

Bankruptcy Cost in the Northern District of Florida

Last updated: 2026-04-18 | Filing fees verified against current US Courts fee schedule.

This page breaks down the real cost of filing bankruptcy in the Northern District of Florida - the federal court covering Florida bankruptcy cases in this region. Filing fees are set nationally by the Judicial Conference and are identical across all 94 federal bankruptcy districts, but attorney fees, case volumes, and dismissal rates vary meaningfully by district. The figures below combine the 2026 court fee schedule with actual case counts pulled from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for this district, plus market-rate attorney fee ranges typical of mid-size metropolitan markets.

Quick answer: In the Northern District of Florida, expect total Chapter 7 costs of roughly $1,468 to $2,938 (filing fee + attorney fee + credit counseling). Chapter 13 filing fee is $313, but total case cost over a 3-5 year plan typically reaches $15,313 or more when plan payments and trustee commission are included.

Federal Filing Fees (2026) - Same Nationwide

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and apply uniformly to every federal bankruptcy district, including the Northern District of Florida. The 2026 amounts are:

ChapterFiling FeeWho Files

Chapter 7$338Individuals seeking liquidation

Chapter 11$1,738Businesses and high-debt individuals

Chapter 12$278Family farmers and fishermen

Chapter 13$313Individuals with regular income

These fees cover clerk services, case administration, and trustee appointment. They do not include attorney fees, credit counseling, or the cost of any required bankruptcy schedules. All four chapters allow installment payment of the filing fee (Form 103A); only Chapter 7 allows a complete fee waiver (Form 103B) for filers below 150% of the federal poverty line.

Attorney Fee Ranges in the Northern District of Florida

Attorney fees are where district-level cost really diverges. The Northern District of Florida is a mid-size metropolitan legal market, which pushes Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 no-look fees into the following typical ranges:

ChapterFiling FeeAttorney Fee RangeTotal Cost Range

Chapter 7$338$1,100 - $2,500$1,468 - $2,938

Chapter 13$313$3,000 - $5,000$3,343 - $5,413

Chapter 11$1,738$10,000 - $40,000$11,768 - $41,838

Total includes credit counseling $30 - $100 for both required courses.

Some bankruptcy courts publish "no-look fee" guidelines - a presumptive reasonable Chapter 13 attorney fee that the court will approve without requiring detailed fee applications. Check the Northern District of Florida's local rules for the current no-look fee amount before signing a retainer. If your attorney's proposed fee exceeds the no-look amount, the attorney must file a fee application, and the court can reduce fees found to be unreasonable (11 U.S.C. section 329, 330). Fees in excess of the disclosed amount can also be disgorged.

In mid-size metropolitan markets, simple Chapter 7 cases with no adversary proceedings and routine exemption claims fall at the low end of the range. Cases with nondischargeability complaints, means-test contests, lien-strip motions, or multiple vehicles push toward the high end. Chapter 13 fees are higher because of the longer case timeline, the plan-confirmation process, and the ongoing trustee-compliance work over three to five years.

Real Filing Volume in the Northern District of Florida (FJC Data)

The table below shows actual case counts and outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database for the Northern District of Florida covering filings from 1998 through 2026. These are real resolved filings, not estimates. Comparing your chapter choice against the dismissal rates here can save you thousands of dollars in wasted fees on a case that never reaches discharge.

ChapterCases FiledShare of FilingsDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 722049.9%99.1%0.9%

Chapter 1181.8%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Chapter 1321348.3%31.2%68.8%

Discharge and dismissal rates are computed on resolved cases only. Pending cases are excluded. Source: FJC Integrated Database (bankruptcy_master.db).

What the Data Says About Filing Here

Consumer filings in the Northern District of Florida split 50% Chapter 7 and 48% Chapter 13, close to the national mix. Filers here have meaningful choice between chapters and should compare total cost carefully.

Chapter 13 completion in the Northern District of Florida is difficult: only 31% of resolved Chapter 13 cases reach discharge. Roughly two-thirds of Chapter 13 filers here pay filing fees, attorney fees, and months (or years) of plan payments - then dismiss without a discharge. That is an expensive outcome. Before choosing Chapter 13 in Florida, weigh this completion rate against the certainty of Chapter 7 discharge for qualifying filers.

Chapter 7 is a high-reliability path in the Northern District of Florida: 99% of resolved Chapter 7 cases reach discharge. For filers who pass the means test, the Chapter 7 filing fee and attorney fee are near-certain to buy an actual discharge rather than a dismissal.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Northern District of Florida. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Florida (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Northern District of Florida - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Northern District of Florida

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Northern District of Florida

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Florida county.

Law school clinics. Several Florida law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Northern District of Florida clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Northern District of Illinois - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Northern District of Illinois

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Northern District of Illinois

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Illinois county.

Law school clinics. Several Illinois law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Northern District of Illinois clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Northern District of Indiana - 2026 filing fees, attorney fees, and real case data

Home » By District » Northern District of Indiana

Bankruptcy Cost in the Northern District of Indiana

Last updated: 2026-04-18 | Filing fees verified against current US Courts fee schedule.

This page breaks down the real cost of filing bankruptcy in the Northern District of Indiana - the federal court covering Indiana bankruptcy cases in this region. Filing fees are set nationally by the Judicial Conference and are identical across all 94 federal bankruptcy districts, but attorney fees, case volumes, and dismissal rates vary meaningfully by district. The figures below combine the 2026 court fee schedule with actual case counts pulled from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for this district, plus market-rate attorney fee ranges typical of mid-size metropolitan markets.

Quick answer: In the Northern District of Indiana, expect total Chapter 7 costs of roughly $1,468 to $2,938 (filing fee + attorney fee + credit counseling). Chapter 13 filing fee is $313, but total case cost over a 3-5 year plan typically reaches $15,313 or more when plan payments and trustee commission are included.

Federal Filing Fees (2026) - Same Nationwide

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and apply uniformly to every federal bankruptcy district, including the Northern District of Indiana. The 2026 amounts are:

ChapterFiling FeeWho Files

Chapter 7$338Individuals seeking liquidation

Chapter 11$1,738Businesses and high-debt individuals

Chapter 12$278Family farmers and fishermen

Chapter 13$313Individuals with regular income

These fees cover clerk services, case administration, and trustee appointment. They do not include attorney fees, credit counseling, or the cost of any required bankruptcy schedules. All four chapters allow installment payment of the filing fee (Form 103A); only Chapter 7 allows a complete fee waiver (Form 103B) for filers below 150% of the federal poverty line.

Attorney Fee Ranges in the Northern District of Indiana

Attorney fees are where district-level cost really diverges. The Northern District of Indiana is a mid-size metropolitan legal market, which pushes Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 no-look fees into the following typical ranges:

ChapterFiling FeeAttorney Fee RangeTotal Cost Range

Chapter 7$338$1,100 - $2,500$1,468 - $2,938

Chapter 13$313$3,000 - $5,000$3,343 - $5,413

Chapter 11$1,738$10,000 - $40,000$11,768 - $41,838

Total includes credit counseling $30 - $100 for both required courses.

Some bankruptcy courts publish "no-look fee" guidelines - a presumptive reasonable Chapter 13 attorney fee that the court will approve without requiring detailed fee applications. Check the Northern District of Indiana's local rules for the current no-look fee amount before signing a retainer. If your attorney's proposed fee exceeds the no-look amount, the attorney must file a fee application, and the court can reduce fees found to be unreasonable (11 U.S.C. section 329, 330). Fees in excess of the disclosed amount can also be disgorged.

In mid-size metropolitan markets, simple Chapter 7 cases with no adversary proceedings and routine exemption claims fall at the low end of the range. Cases with nondischargeability complaints, means-test contests, lien-strip motions, or multiple vehicles push toward the high end. Chapter 13 fees are higher because of the longer case timeline, the plan-confirmation process, and the ongoing trustee-compliance work over three to five years.

Real Filing Volume in the Northern District of Indiana (FJC Data)

The table below shows actual case counts and outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database for the Northern District of Indiana covering filings from 1991 through 2026. These are real resolved filings, not estimates. Comparing your chapter choice against the dismissal rates here can save you thousands of dollars in wasted fees on a case that never reaches discharge.

ChapterCases FiledShare of FilingsDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 730320.4%100.0%0.0%

Chapter 11644.3%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Chapter 131,11875.3%64.6%35.2%

Discharge and dismissal rates are computed on resolved cases only. Pending cases are excluded. Source: FJC Integrated Database (bankruptcy_master.db).

What the Data Says About Filing Here

The Northern District of Indiana is a Chapter-13-heavy jurisdiction: 75% of consumer filings are Chapter 13 repayment plans versus 20% Chapter 7. Some districts push debtors toward Chapter 13 through local practice norms, trustee policies, or attorney-fee incentives (Chapter 13 no-look fees paid through the plan are attractive to filers who cannot pay Chapter 7 fees up front). Filers here should run the total-cost math on both chapters before deciding - Chapter 13 attorney fees are paid through the plan but are almost always larger in total than Chapter 7 fees paid up front.

Chapter 13 completion in the Northern District of Indiana is strong: 65% of resolved cases reach discharge - above the national norm. Plans that run to completion are the majority here, which meaningfully raises the cost-effectiveness of Chapter 13 as a repayment path.

Chapter 7 is a high-reliability path in the Northern District of Indiana: 100% of resolved Chapter 7 cases reach discharge. For filers who pass the means test, the Chapter 7 filing fee and attorney fee are near-certain to buy an actual discharge rather than a dismissal.

The district also handles a meaningful Chapter 11 docket (64 cases in the sample), including individual Chapter 11 and Subchapter V small-business cases. Chapter 11 costs are an order of magnitude higher than consumer chapters - the filing fee alone is $1,738, and attorney fees typically start at five figures.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Northern District of Indiana. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Indiana (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Northern District of Indiana - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Northern District of Indiana

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Northern District of Indiana

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Indiana county.

Law school clinics. Several Indiana law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Northern District of Indiana clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Northern District of Texas - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Northern District of Texas

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Northern District of Texas

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Texas county.

Law school clinics. Several Texas law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Northern District of Texas clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Southern District of California - 2026 filing fees, attorney fees, and real case data

Home » By District » Southern District of California

Bankruptcy Cost in the Southern District of California

Last updated: 2026-04-18 | Filing fees verified against current US Courts fee schedule.

This page breaks down the real cost of filing bankruptcy in the Southern District of California - the federal court covering California bankruptcy cases in this region. Filing fees are set nationally by the Judicial Conference and are identical across all 94 federal bankruptcy districts, but attorney fees, case volumes, and dismissal rates vary meaningfully by district. The figures below combine the 2026 court fee schedule with actual case counts pulled from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for this district, plus market-rate attorney fee ranges typical of major metropolitan markets.

Quick answer: In the Southern District of California, expect total Chapter 7 costs of roughly $1,868 to $3,938 (filing fee + attorney fee + credit counseling). Chapter 13 filing fee is $313, but total case cost over a 3-5 year plan typically reaches $17,813 or more when plan payments and trustee commission are included.

Federal Filing Fees (2026) - Same Nationwide

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and apply uniformly to every federal bankruptcy district, including the Southern District of California. The 2026 amounts are:

ChapterFiling FeeWho Files

Chapter 7$338Individuals seeking liquidation

Chapter 11$1,738Businesses and high-debt individuals

Chapter 12$278Family farmers and fishermen

Chapter 13$313Individuals with regular income

These fees cover clerk services, case administration, and trustee appointment. They do not include attorney fees, credit counseling, or the cost of any required bankruptcy schedules. All four chapters allow installment payment of the filing fee (Form 103A); only Chapter 7 allows a complete fee waiver (Form 103B) for filers below 150% of the federal poverty line.

Attorney Fee Ranges in the Southern District of California

Attorney fees are where district-level cost really diverges. The Southern District of California is a major metropolitan legal market, which pushes Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 no-look fees into the following typical ranges:

ChapterFiling FeeAttorney Fee RangeTotal Cost Range

Chapter 7$338$1,500 - $3,500$1,868 - $3,938

Chapter 13$313$3,500 - $6,500$3,843 - $6,913

Chapter 11$1,738$15,000 - $60,000$16,768 - $61,838

Total includes credit counseling $30 - $100 for both required courses.

Some bankruptcy courts publish "no-look fee" guidelines - a presumptive reasonable Chapter 13 attorney fee that the court will approve without requiring detailed fee applications. Check the Southern District of California's local rules for the current no-look fee amount before signing a retainer. If your attorney's proposed fee exceeds the no-look amount, the attorney must file a fee application, and the court can reduce fees found to be unreasonable (11 U.S.C. section 329, 330). Fees in excess of the disclosed amount can also be disgorged.

In major metropolitan markets, simple Chapter 7 cases with no adversary proceedings and routine exemption claims fall at the low end of the range. Cases with nondischargeability complaints, means-test contests, lien-strip motions, or multiple vehicles push toward the high end. Chapter 13 fees are higher because of the longer case timeline, the plan-confirmation process, and the ongoing trustee-compliance work over three to five years.

Real Filing Volume in the Southern District of California (FJC Data)

The table below shows actual case counts and outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database for the Southern District of California covering filings from 1988 through 2024. These are real resolved filings, not estimates. Comparing your chapter choice against the dismissal rates here can save you thousands of dollars in wasted fees on a case that never reaches discharge.

ChapterCases FiledShare of FilingsDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 74970.0%97.7%2.3%

Chapter 1111.4%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Chapter 132028.6%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Discharge and dismissal rates are computed on resolved cases only. Pending cases are excluded. Source: FJC Integrated Database (bankruptcy_master.db).

What the Data Says About Filing Here

The Southern District of California is a Chapter-7-heavy jurisdiction: 70% of consumer filings here are Chapter 7 liquidations versus 29% for Chapter 13 repayment plans. This matters for cost planning because Chapter 7 is the lower-total-cost path when you qualify - a single filing fee, a one-time attorney fee, and a 90-day case timeline versus three-to-five years of plan payments in Chapter 13.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Southern District of California. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in California (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Southern District of California - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Southern District of California

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Southern District of California

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your California county.

Law school clinics. Several California law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Southern District of California clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Indiana (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Southern District of Indiana - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Southern District of Indiana

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Southern District of Indiana

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Indiana county.

Law school clinics. Several Indiana law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Southern District of Indiana clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Southern District of Ohio - 2026 filing fees, attorney fees, and real case data

Home » By District » Southern District of Ohio

Bankruptcy Cost in the Southern District of Ohio

Last updated: 2026-04-18 | Filing fees verified against current US Courts fee schedule.

This page breaks down the real cost of filing bankruptcy in the Southern District of Ohio - the federal court covering Ohio bankruptcy cases in this region. Filing fees are set nationally by the Judicial Conference and are identical across all 94 federal bankruptcy districts, but attorney fees, case volumes, and dismissal rates vary meaningfully by district. The figures below combine the 2026 court fee schedule with actual case counts pulled from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for this district, plus market-rate attorney fee ranges typical of mid-size metropolitan markets.

Quick answer: In the Southern District of Ohio, expect total Chapter 7 costs of roughly $1,468 to $2,938 (filing fee + attorney fee + credit counseling). Chapter 13 filing fee is $313, but total case cost over a 3-5 year plan typically reaches $15,313 or more when plan payments and trustee commission are included.

Federal Filing Fees (2026) - Same Nationwide

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and apply uniformly to every federal bankruptcy district, including the Southern District of Ohio. The 2026 amounts are:

ChapterFiling FeeWho Files

Chapter 7$338Individuals seeking liquidation

Chapter 11$1,738Businesses and high-debt individuals

Chapter 12$278Family farmers and fishermen

Chapter 13$313Individuals with regular income

These fees cover clerk services, case administration, and trustee appointment. They do not include attorney fees, credit counseling, or the cost of any required bankruptcy schedules. All four chapters allow installment payment of the filing fee (Form 103A); only Chapter 7 allows a complete fee waiver (Form 103B) for filers below 150% of the federal poverty line.

Attorney Fee Ranges in the Southern District of Ohio

Attorney fees are where district-level cost really diverges. The Southern District of Ohio is a mid-size metropolitan legal market, which pushes Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 no-look fees into the following typical ranges:

ChapterFiling FeeAttorney Fee RangeTotal Cost Range

Chapter 7$338$1,100 - $2,500$1,468 - $2,938

Chapter 13$313$3,000 - $5,000$3,343 - $5,413

Chapter 11$1,738$10,000 - $40,000$11,768 - $41,838

Total includes credit counseling $30 - $100 for both required courses.

Some bankruptcy courts publish "no-look fee" guidelines - a presumptive reasonable Chapter 13 attorney fee that the court will approve without requiring detailed fee applications. Check the Southern District of Ohio's local rules for the current no-look fee amount before signing a retainer. If your attorney's proposed fee exceeds the no-look amount, the attorney must file a fee application, and the court can reduce fees found to be unreasonable (11 U.S.C. section 329, 330). Fees in excess of the disclosed amount can also be disgorged.

In mid-size metropolitan markets, simple Chapter 7 cases with no adversary proceedings and routine exemption claims fall at the low end of the range. Cases with nondischargeability complaints, means-test contests, lien-strip motions, or multiple vehicles push toward the high end. Chapter 13 fees are higher because of the longer case timeline, the plan-confirmation process, and the ongoing trustee-compliance work over three to five years.

Real Filing Volume in the Southern District of Ohio (FJC Data)

The table below shows actual case counts and outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database for the Southern District of Ohio covering filings from 1991 through 2026. These are real resolved filings, not estimates. Comparing your chapter choice against the dismissal rates here can save you thousands of dollars in wasted fees on a case that never reaches discharge.

ChapterCases FiledShare of FilingsDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 728549.3%100.0%0.0%

Chapter 1113022.5%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Chapter 1316328.2%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Discharge and dismissal rates are computed on resolved cases only. Pending cases are excluded. Source: FJC Integrated Database (bankruptcy_master.db).

What the Data Says About Filing Here

Consumer filings in the Southern District of Ohio split 49% Chapter 7 and 28% Chapter 13, close to the national mix. Filers here have meaningful choice between chapters and should compare total cost carefully.

The district also handles a meaningful Chapter 11 docket (130 cases in the sample), including individual Chapter 11 and Subchapter V small-business cases. Chapter 11 costs are an order of magnitude higher than consumer chapters - the filing fee alone is $1,738, and attorney fees typically start at five figures.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Southern District of Ohio. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Ohio (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Southern District of Ohio - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Southern District of Ohio

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Southern District of Ohio

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Ohio county.

Law school clinics. Several Ohio law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Southern District of Ohio clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Arkansas (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Western District of Arkansas - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Western District of Arkansas

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Western District of Arkansas

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Arkansas county.

Law school clinics. Several Arkansas law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Western District of Arkansas clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Western District of Kentucky - 2026 filing fees, attorney fees, and real case data

Bankruptcy Cost in the Western District of Kentucky

Last updated: 2026-04-18 | Filing fees verified against current US Courts fee schedule.

This page breaks down the real cost of filing bankruptcy in the Western District of Kentucky - the federal court covering Kentucky bankruptcy cases in this region. Filing fees are set nationally by the Judicial Conference and are identical across all 94 federal bankruptcy districts, but attorney fees, case volumes, and dismissal rates vary meaningfully by district. The figures below combine the 2026 court fee schedule with actual case counts pulled from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for this district, plus market-rate attorney fee ranges typical of mid-size metropolitan markets.

Quick answer: In the Western District of Kentucky, expect total Chapter 7 costs of roughly $1,468 to $2,938 (filing fee + attorney fee + credit counseling). Chapter 13 filing fee is $313, but total case cost over a 3-5 year plan typically reaches $15,313 or more when plan payments and trustee commission are included.

Federal Filing Fees (2026) - Same Nationwide

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and apply uniformly to every federal bankruptcy district, including the Western District of Kentucky. The 2026 amounts are:

ChapterFiling FeeWho Files

Chapter 7$338Individuals seeking liquidation

Chapter 11$1,738Businesses and high-debt individuals

Chapter 12$278Family farmers and fishermen

Chapter 13$313Individuals with regular income

These fees cover clerk services, case administration, and trustee appointment. They do not include attorney fees, credit counseling, or the cost of any required bankruptcy schedules. All four chapters allow installment payment of the filing fee (Form 103A); only Chapter 7 allows a complete fee waiver (Form 103B) for filers below 150% of the federal poverty line.

Attorney Fee Ranges in the Western District of Kentucky

Attorney fees are where district-level cost really diverges. The Western District of Kentucky is a mid-size metropolitan legal market, which pushes Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 no-look fees into the following typical ranges:

ChapterFiling FeeAttorney Fee RangeTotal Cost Range

Chapter 7$338$1,100 - $2,500$1,468 - $2,938

Chapter 13$313$3,000 - $5,000$3,343 - $5,413

Chapter 11$1,738$10,000 - $40,000$11,768 - $41,838

Total includes credit counseling $30 - $100 for both required courses.

Some bankruptcy courts publish "no-look fee" guidelines - a presumptive reasonable Chapter 13 attorney fee that the court will approve without requiring detailed fee applications. Check the Western District of Kentucky's local rules for the current no-look fee amount before signing a retainer. If your attorney's proposed fee exceeds the no-look amount, the attorney must file a fee application, and the court can reduce fees found to be unreasonable (11 U.S.C. section 329, 330). Fees in excess of the disclosed amount can also be disgorged.

In mid-size metropolitan markets, simple Chapter 7 cases with no adversary proceedings and routine exemption claims fall at the low end of the range. Cases with nondischargeability complaints, means-test contests, lien-strip motions, or multiple vehicles push toward the high end. Chapter 13 fees are higher because of the longer case timeline, the plan-confirmation process, and the ongoing trustee-compliance work over three to five years.

Real Filing Volume in the Western District of Kentucky (FJC Data)

The table below shows actual case counts and outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database for the Western District of Kentucky covering filings from 1992 through 2024. These are real resolved filings, not estimates. Comparing your chapter choice against the dismissal rates here can save you thousands of dollars in wasted fees on a case that never reaches discharge.

ChapterCases FiledShare of FilingsDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7294.7%96.3%3.7%

Chapter 1120.3%Insufficient dataInsufficient data

Chapter 1358495.0%67.8%32.2%

Discharge and dismissal rates are computed on resolved cases only. Pending cases are excluded. Source: FJC Integrated Database (bankruptcy_master.db).

What the Data Says About Filing Here

The Western District of Kentucky is a Chapter-13-heavy jurisdiction: 95% of consumer filings are Chapter 13 repayment plans versus 5% Chapter 7. Some districts push debtors toward Chapter 13 through local practice norms, trustee policies, or attorney-fee incentives (Chapter 13 no-look fees paid through the plan are attractive to filers who cannot pay Chapter 7 fees up front). Filers here should run the total-cost math on both chapters before deciding - Chapter 13 attorney fees are paid through the plan but are almost always larger in total than Chapter 7 fees paid up front.

Chapter 13 completion in the Western District of Kentucky is strong: 68% of resolved cases reach discharge - above the national norm. Plans that run to completion are the majority here, which meaningfully raises the cost-effectiveness of Chapter 13 as a repayment path.

Chapter 7 is a high-reliability path in the Western District of Kentucky: 96% of resolved Chapter 7 cases reach discharge. For filers who pass the means test, the Chapter 7 filing fee and attorney fee are near-certain to buy an actual discharge rather than a dismissal.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Western District of Kentucky. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Kentucky (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Hidden Costs Specific to the Western District of Kentucky

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Western District of Kentucky

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Kentucky county.

Law school clinics. Several Kentucky law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Western District of Kentucky clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.

Roughly two-thirds of Chapter 13 filers here pay filing fees, attorney fees, and months (or years) of plan payments - then dismiss without a discharge. That is an expensive outcome. Before choosing Chapter 13 in Tennessee, weigh this completion rate against the certainty of Chapter 7 discharge for qualifying filers.

Chapter 7 is a high-reliability path in the Western District of Tennessee: 96% of resolved Chapter 7 cases reach discharge. For filers who pass the means test, the Chapter 7 filing fee and attorney fee are near-certain to buy an actual discharge rather than a dismissal.

The district also handles a meaningful Chapter 11 docket (121 cases in the sample), including individual Chapter 11 and Subchapter V small-business cases. Chapter 11 costs are an order of magnitude higher than consumer chapters - the filing fee alone is $1,738, and attorney fees typically start at five figures.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Total Cost Math

The sticker price of Chapter 13 looks lower than Chapter 7 because the filing fee is $25 less. That comparison is misleading. Chapter 13 is a three-to-five-year repayment plan, and the total cost of a Chapter 13 case - filing fee plus attorney fee plus plan payments plus trustee commission - is almost always larger than Chapter 7.

Here is the math for a typical mid-range Chapter 13 case in the Western District of Tennessee. Assume a filing fee of $313, an attorney fee paid through the plan of $4,500 (mid-market), and a 60-month plan with monthly payments of $400. The debtor pays the filing fee up front, then pays $400 per month for 60 months = $24,000 total into the plan. The trustee takes a 10% commission ($2,400). The attorney fee of $4,500 is paid from plan payments. After the trustee commission, roughly $17,100 flows to creditors. The debtor's total out-of-pocket across the case: filing fee + 60 payments = $313 + $24,000 = $24,313.

Compare that to Chapter 7 at the same market rate: $338 filing fee + $1,800 attorney fee + $60 counseling = $2,198 total, paid once. For a qualifying filer, Chapter 7 is roughly 1/10 the total cost.

Chapter 13 is still the right chapter for filers who (a) fail the means test, (b) need to cure mortgage arrears to save a home, or (c) have nondischargeable priority tax debt to pay over time. But the cost comparison should drive the decision, not the $25 filing-fee gap.

Chapter 7 Fee Waiver in Tennessee (Form 103B)

The $338 Chapter 7 filing fee can be waived entirely if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. The waiver is available only in Chapter 7 - not Chapter 11, 12, or 13 - because those chapters contemplate ongoing payments. File Form 103B with your petition.

Household Size150% Poverty (Annual)Monthly Equivalent

1 person$22,590$1,882

2 persons$30,660$2,555

3 persons$38,730$3,228

4 persons$46,800$3,900

5 persons$54,870$4,572

6 persons$62,940$5,245

If you are above 150% of poverty but cannot pay the filing fee in a lump sum, use Form 103A to pay in up to four installments over 120 days. You cannot pay an attorney while paying the filing fee in installments.

Credit Counseling and Debtor Education

Every consumer bankruptcy filer - in every district, including the Western District of Tennessee - must complete two credit courses: a pre-filing credit counseling briefing (within 180 days before filing) and a post-filing debtor education course (before discharge). Both courses are provided by DOJ-approved nonprofit agencies, typically online. Fees run $30 to $100 per course and can be waived for low-income filers. The DOJ publishes a list of approved providers; compare prices and hardship-waiver policies before enrolling.

Hidden Costs Specific to the Western District of Tennessee

Beyond filing fees, attorney fees, and counseling, several costs frequently surprise first-time filers here:

Amendment fees. Amending schedules after filing often carries a fee (around $34). If you forget a creditor or misstate an asset, the fix costs money.

Reaffirmation hearings. If you reaffirm a vehicle loan or mortgage in Chapter 7, you may need to attend a reaffirmation hearing. Attorneys sometimes charge extra for this.

341 meeting travel. The 341 meeting of creditors is held in person in many districts. If you live far from the meeting location, factor in travel time and cost.

Trustee fees in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 trustees take a commission (typically 4-10%) on every dollar that flows through the plan. A $24,000 plan can carry $1,500-$2,400 in trustee commissions.

Lien-strip and valuation motions. If you need to strip a wholly-unsecured junior mortgage or a lien on a vehicle, your attorney may charge separately for the motion and any required valuation evidence.

A good attorney will quote these as part of the retainer rather than billing them a-la-carte after filing. Ask about them up front.

Free and Low-Cost Options in the Western District of Tennessee

Several pathways exist for filers who cannot afford standard retainer fees in this district:

Legal Services Corporation legal aid. Search LawHelp.org by state and filter to bankruptcy. LSC-funded legal aid offices represent qualifying low-income filers at no cost.

Local bar association pro bono panels. Many county bar associations maintain panels of private attorneys who accept bankruptcy cases at no charge. Call the local bar in your Tennessee county.

Law school clinics. Several Tennessee law schools operate supervised bankruptcy clinics. Work is handled by law students under faculty supervision, and the service is free.

Pro se filing. For simple Chapter 7 cases with no real estate, few assets, and no adversary proceedings, pro se filing is viable. The Western District of Tennessee clerk's office publishes pro se filing packets. Pro se Chapter 13 is strongly discouraged - dismissal rates run much higher than for represented cases.
